Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio

Visual Analytics for Profitability & Volatility Discovery

ZeXin Chen

2026-05-14

  • About the data
  • Key variables & derived metrics

Part 2: Portfolio Composition

  • Policy & geographic breakdown

  • Claim frequency patterns

Good morning everyone. Today I will be walking you through an exploratory visual analysis of a real motor insurance portfolio from Spain. The dataset covers three years of policy transactions and gives us a great opportunity to look at what actually drives profitability and claims volatility in a non-life insurance book. We will move through four parts: first some context on the data, then a look at the portfolio makeup, followed by profitability findings, and finally what is driving volatility.

Part 1: Dataset Overview

About the Dataset

Source: Spanish motor insurer microdata
Period: January 2022 – December 2024
Records: 354,140 policy transactions
Variables: 47 across 4 groups

Group Variables
Policy & Insured 8
Driver & Vehicle 10
Premiums 8
Claims & Incurred 21

Three derived metrics guide analysis:

\[\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Premium}}\]

\[\text{Claim Freq} = \frac{\text{Claims}}{\text{Exposure}}\]

\[\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Claims}}\]

Note

Loss Ratio < 1 = Profitable
Loss Ratio > 1 = Unprofitable

So what are we working with? This is real anonymised data from a Spanish motor insurer, covering about 354,000 policy transactions over three years. Each row represents one policy in one year. The three metrics on the right are what we will use throughout the presentation. Loss ratio is our profitability measure. Anything below 1 means the insurer made money on that policy. Claim frequency tells us how often accidents happen per year of exposure. Severity tells us how costly each claim is when it does happen.

Data Quality

  • fuel_type: 0.37% missing (1,311 records) — excluded when fuel type is analysed
  • vehicle_value: 0.14% missing (500 records) — excluded when vehicle value is analysed
  • All other 45 variables are 100% complete

Good news on data quality. Out of 47 variables, only two have any missing values at all. Fuel type is missing for less than half a percent of records, and vehicle value for just 0.14 percent. Everything else is complete and clean, which is quite rare for a real-world dataset of this size.

Part 2: Portfolio Composition

Insight 1: CC Policies Dominate the Portfolio

  • CC (Third-party + add-ons) is the dominant policy at 57.8% of the portfolio
  • COMP_E (Comprehensive with excess) is second at 25.8%
  • Basic TP (Third-party only) is rare at just 1.6% — most customers prefer broader coverage

CC policies dominate at 58 percent. These are third-party liability combined with several add-ons like theft and glass. COMP_E at 26 percent is full comprehensive with an excess. What stands out is how rare basic TP policies are at just 1.6 percent. This tells us the insurer is largely serving customers who want broader protection.

Insight 2: Portfolio is Stable with Low-Risk Customers

  • 89.2% of policies are active; cancellation rate of 10.8% warrants monitoring
  • 96.4% of customers have a Good bonus score — no recent claims history
  • Bad-score customers are only 1.3% of the portfolio but are a key risk segment

On the left, 89 percent of policies are active and 11 percent cancelled. On the right, the bonus score is striking. 96 percent of customers have a Good score, meaning they have had no recent claims. This is very positive for profitability. But it also means the Bad group at 1.3 percent is very small so we need to be careful drawing conclusions from it statistically.

Insight 3: Experienced Drivers, Older Vehicles

  • Most drivers are aged 40-60 years — an experienced, lower-risk segment
  • Vehicle age peaks at 15-35 years — an older fleet than typical
  • Vehicle values concentrate between €15k-€40k with a high-value tail

Three things jump out from these charts. First, the typical driver here is in their mid-40s to mid-50s. Very few young drivers under 25 appear in this book. Second, the vehicles are quite old with many in the 15 to 35 year range. Third, vehicle values mostly sit between 15 and 40 thousand euros, but there are expensive vehicles in the tail that can generate very large claims.

Insight 4: Urban-Heavy, Inland-Dominant Portfolio

  • 64.6% of policies are in inland municipalities; islands account for only 6.8%
  • Urban and rural circulation are split 53.8% vs 46.2% — near equal exposure
  • 64.2% of vehicles use diesel — relevant for repair cost patterns

The geographic mix shows inland as the dominant segment at 65 percent. Urban and rural circulation are fairly balanced. Diesel vehicles make up 64 percent of the fleet. These splits matter because urban and rural drivers have very different claim frequencies as we will see shortly.

Part 3: Profitability Analysis

Insight 5: 88% of Policies Have Zero Claims

  • 88.1% of policies generate zero claims; only 11.9% file any claim
  • Among claimants, the distribution peaks near LR = 0.1-0.3 and decays toward break-even
  • 9.0% of all policies exceed break-even (LR > 1) — these drive total portfolio losses

I have split this into two panels. On the left, 88 percent of policies never filed a single claim. On the right, we look only at the claimants. The distribution peaks near 0.1 to 0.3 and decays toward the break-even line. Only 9 percent of all policies exceed break-even. These are the policies that really matter for the portfolio bottom line.

Insight 6: Comprehensive Policies Have Higher Loss Ratios

  • COMP_E median LR = 0.92; COMP_N median LR = 0.90 — highest among all types
  • CC median LR = 0.91; TPG = 0.98; TP = 0.68 — basic coverage has lower loss ratios
  • Comprehensive policies show the widest IQR, indicating greater profitability volatility

With the axis capped at 2 and using boxplots, the differences are clearly visible. COMP_E and COMP_N sit higher than TP and basic coverage types. The boxplot shows that comprehensive policies not only have higher medians but also much wider spreads, confirming they are the main source of profitability uncertainty.

Insight 7: Bad Claims History Predicts Higher Loss Ratios

  • Bad-score median LR = 0.67; IQR = 0.31-1.05 — wider and higher than Good
  • Good-score median LR = 0.72; IQR = 0.35-1.10 — tighter distribution
  • Bad-score policyholders represent only 1.3% of portfolio but show greater loss volatility

The Bad-score violin highlighted in blue is noticeably wider than the grey Good group. This confirms the bonus-malus system is working correctly. It identifies riskier customers. Even though the Bad group is only 1.3 percent of the portfolio, their loss distribution is more spread out, contributing disproportionately to aggregate volatility.

Insight 8: Comprehensive Policies Cost More Per Claim

  • COMP_E mean severity = €891 per claim; COMP_N = €793
  • CC mean severity = €821; TP = €928 (high due to small sample)
  • Wide IQR across all types confirms individual claim costs are highly unpredictable

Not only do comprehensive policies have more claims, but each claim also costs more. COMP_E and COMP_N show the highest and most variable severity distributions. The wide interquartile range across all policy types tells us that predicting how much any individual claim will cost is genuinely difficult regardless of policy type.

Part 4: Volatility Analysis

Insight 9: Young Drivers File Claims 2.7x More Often

  • Drivers aged 19-25 have mean claim frequency of 0.716 — highest of all groups
  • Drivers aged 56-65 average only 0.289 — the safest segment
  • The 19-25 group files claims 2.7x more often than the 56-65 group

This chart shows a pattern actuaries know well. The youngest drivers from 19 to 25 have the highest claim frequency at 0.716 by a clear margin. Then it drops steadily through the middle age groups. The 19-25 group files claims 2.7 times more often than the safest group. One note: the 19-25 bar is based on a relatively small sample as very few young drivers appear in this portfolio.

Insight 10: Urban Inland Drivers Have Highest Claim Rates

  • Inland Urban: mean frequency = 0.371 — highest among all combinations
  • Coastal Urban: 0.314 vs Coastal Rural: 0.284 — urban always higher
  • Urban drivers consistently file 10-25% more claims than rural across all regions

Urban drivers consistently file more claims than rural drivers across all three municipality types. Inland urban shows the highest frequency at 0.371. The blue bars are always taller than the grey bars within each municipality type. The urban vs rural gap is consistent across all regions, confirming that circulation area is a strong predictor of claim volatility.

Insight 11: COMP_N Loss Ratio Rose to 1.17 by 2024

  • COMP_N rose from 0.71 (2022) to 1.17 (2024) — crossed break-even in 2024
  • COMP_E rose from 0.64 (2022) to 1.11 (2024) — also crossed break-even
  • TP, TPG, CC remain below break-even — basic coverage types remain profitable

This is arguably the most alarming finding. COMP_N and COMP_E both crossed the break-even line in 2024. COMP_N went from 0.71 in 2022 to 1.17 in 2024. This means the insurer is now paying out more in claims than it collects in premiums for these policy types. This could indicate rising repair costs or medical inflation. Basic coverage types remain comfortably below break-even throughout the period.

Key Findings Summary

Profitability Drivers

  • 🔵 Policy Type: COMP_E/COMP_N crossed break-even in 2024
  • 🔵 Trend: COMP_N LR rose from 0.71 to 1.17 (2022-2024)
  • ⬜ Bonus Score: Bad-score holders have wider loss distributions
  • ⬜ 88.1% of policies have zero claims

Volatility Drivers

  • 🔵 Young Drivers: 19-25 group has 2.7x higher claim frequency
  • 🔵 Urban Circulation: Inland Urban frequency = 0.371 (highest)
  • ⬜ Geography: Urban always higher than rural in all regions
  • ⬜ Claim severity highly variable within each policy type

Important

Core finding: 88.1% of policies have zero claims. The portfolio’s entire profitability challenge comes from 9% of policies that exceed break-even — and comprehensive policies are now crossing that line.

To wrap up. COMP_E and COMP_N have crossed break-even in 2024 — this is the most actionable finding. On volatility, young drivers file claims 2.7 times more than the safest group. Urban circulation consistently drives higher frequencies. The overarching finding is that 88 percent of policies never generate a claim. The challenge is managing the small but growing share of loss-making comprehensive policies.
